title: Trade and Income -- Exploiting Time Series in Geography
research_question: Does an increase in international trade raise national income per capita, and how large is the elasticity of income with respect to trade? Specifically, can changes in cross-country trade volumes account for differences in long-run income growth across countries?
data_description: Bilateral trade data come from the IMF Direction of Trade database (via Glick and Taylor 2008), covering country pairs from 1950 to 1997, used at five-year intervals. Real GDP per capita and per worker are from the Penn World Tables (version 6.1/6.2), spanning 1960-1995 for roughly 101 countries (62 in a balanced subsample). Bilateral great-circle distances and pair-level controls (contiguity, common language, colonial links) are from CEPII; bilateral sea distances were constructed by the author using 1x1 degree gridded geographic data (CIESIN) and ocean current data (NCAR), computing shortest shipping routes between primary ports at 20 knots. Additional data include US Census Bureau HS-category air/sea import shares for 2001, UNIDO manufacturing data, and UN National Accounts industrial structure data for 1970. Landlocked countries and oil exporters are excluded. The unit of observation is country-year (and country-pair-year for the bilateral trade stage).
institutional_context: The setting is the post-1950 transformation of international shipping driven by the rise of commercial air freight. Between 1955 and 2004, the price of air freight per ton fell roughly tenfold, while ocean freight costs declined more slowly. As a result, the share of US trade (excluding Canada and Mexico) carried by air rose from negligible levels before 1960 to over half of exports and 30 percent of imports by 2004. Air transport is concentrated in high-value-to-weight goods such as electronics, pharmaceuticals, precious metals, and luxury items, and is used by countries at varying development levels. Because land masses force ocean shipping along circuitous routes while aircraft travel approximately great-circle paths, technological improvements in aviation differentially shortened effective distances for country pairs whose sea routes are long relative to their air routes (e.g., Japan-Germany), reshaping bilateral trade opportunities heterogeneously across countries.
